title: Sliding window
summary: Turn nested loops into one linear pass: expand right, shrink left, update the answer.

clips.title: Why a window?
clips.question: Why does a sliding window beat nested loops?

scenes.say: Sliding window, question one. Why does a sliding window beat nested loops? Pause and answer out loud.

props.question: Why does a sliding window beat nested loops?

scenes.say: Brute force recomputes every window from scratch: a nested loop costing O of N times k, or O of N squared. A sliding window reuses work. When the window moves one step, add the element that enters and remove the one that leaves. Each element enters once and leaves once, so the whole scan is O of N.

left.label: Brute force
left.title: O(N·k)
left.body: Every window is summed from scratch.

right.label: Sliding window
right.title: O(N)
right.body: One add and one remove per step.

verdict.text: Each element enters once and leaves once.

scenes.say: Take a fixed window of three. The first sum is eight. Slide right: add one, drop two, and the sum is seven. Slide again: nine. Then six. The best window sums to nine.

props.title: A fixed window of three
props.problem: Maximum sum of any 3 consecutive elements

steps.note: Add the entering 1, drop the leaving 2

scenes.say: Windows come in two shapes. Fixed size, where k never changes and the window simply slides. And variable size, where the window grows and shrinks to satisfy a constraint. Interviews mostly ask the variable kind.

items.label: Fixed size
items.title: k stays constant
items.body: Slide by one: add the entering element, remove the leaving one.

items.label: Variable size
items.title: Grows and shrinks
items.body: Expand right; shrink left while a constraint is violated.

clips.title: Expand, shrink, update
clips.question: What are the four moves of a variable-size sliding window?

scenes.say: Question two. What are the four moves of a variable-size sliding window? Pause and answer out loud.

props.question: What are the four moves of a variable-size window?

scenes.say: Initialize left and right at zero. Expand by moving right to include a new element. Shrink by moving left while the window violates the constraint. Then update the best answer from the valid window.

items.title: Expand
items.body: Move right to include a new element.

items.title: Shrink
items.body: Move left while the window is invalid.

items.title: Update
items.body: Record the answer from a valid window.

scenes.say: Find the longest substring without repeating characters. Right expands over the first three letters, so the window is three long. The next letter repeats the first one, and the window is invalid. Left shrinks past the old copy, and the window is valid again. The same thing happens at each repeat. At the double letter, left has to move twice. The best length is three.

steps.note: Shrink: left drops the old a
Repeat b → expand, then shrink once
Repeat c → expand, then shrink once
Shrink twice: drop a, then b

scenes.say: Both pointers only ever move forward. That is why the scan stays linear, even with a while loop inside the for loop.

props.sub: The inner while loop is amortized: at most N shrinks in total, so the scan is O(N).

clips.title: The C++ template
clips.question: Write the general variable-size sliding window template from memory.

scenes.say: Question three. Write the general variable-size sliding window template from memory. Pause, and sketch it out.

props.question: Write the variable-size window template from memory.

scenes.say: Here is the template, made concrete for the longest substring without repeats. Keep the window state, here a count map, plus left and the best answer. The for loop moves right and adds the incoming element. The while loop shrinks from the left until the window is valid again, undoing each outgoing element. Finally, update the answer with the window length: right minus left plus one. Swap the state and the condition, and the same skeleton solves most variable-window problems.

props.title: One skeleton, many problems

highlights.note: Expand: right moves, incoming element is added
Shrink while invalid, undoing the outgoing element
Swap state + condition for a new problem

scenes.say: For the state, use a hash map for general keys, a fixed array indexed by character code, which is faster, or a plain integer when you only need a sum or a count.

items.label: Sum or count
items.title: Plain integer
items.body: When one number describes the window.

clips.title: Max vs min: where to update
clips.question: For a maximum window and a minimum window, where does the update go?

scenes.say: Question four. For a maximum window and for a minimum window, where does the result update go? Pause and answer out loud.

props.question: Maximum window, minimum window: where does the update go?

scenes.say: For the longest, or maximum window, shrink until the window is valid, then update after the loop. For the shortest, or minimum window, the loop runs while the window is valid, so update inside it, before each shrink makes the window smaller.

left.label: Maximum window
left.title: After the shrink loop

right.label: Minimum window
right.title: Inside the shrink loop
right.body: Measure each valid window before it shrinks.

verdict.text: Max: update after shrinking. Min: update inside.

scenes.say: Find the shortest subarray with a sum of at least seven. Expand right until the sum reaches eight. That window is valid, so record its length, four, and shrink. Expand again, and the sum is ten. Record, shrink, and the sum is still seven, so record three. Expand to the end, and the sum is nine. Shrink once: still seven. Record two, the answer.

To recap. Reuse work instead of recomputing. Expand right, shrink left, update the answer. Both pointers only move forward, so it is linear. And for the update: maximum goes after the shrink loop, minimum goes inside it.

items.text: Reuse work: add what enters, remove what leaves.
Expand right, shrink left, update the answer.
Max: update after shrinking. Min: update inside.
